_comment: Two analytical classifications of the CPI expenditure classes. Neither is
a published ABS series -- both are judgements, and different houses draw
them differently, which is exactly why they live here as data you can edit
rather than in the code as constants you cannot.
Names must match the ABS expenditure-class names exactly, as they appear
in the Data tab's class list. Anything not named below falls into the
residual bucket ('Other' for composition, 'non-cyclical' for the cycle
split) rather than being dropped, so a gap shows up as a fat residual on
screen instead of a quietly short bar.
Order matters for `composition`: a class is claimed by the FIRST bucket
that lists it, which is how 'Fuel' takes automotive fuel out of tradables
and 'Tobacco' takes tobacco out of administered prices.
Buckets for the quarterly seasonally adjusted contributions chart. The
split follows the RBA's own analytical language: administered prices are
the classes whose price is set or heavily shaped by government rather
than by a market; tradables are the classes exposed to world prices and
the exchange rate; domestic market services are the labour-intensive
services where domestic wages do most of the work. Rent and new dwelling
purchase are pulled out on their own because they are the housing
channel the cash rate acts on most directly.
Administered prices ex tobacco: Other services in respect of motor vehicles
Tradables ex fuel: Ice cream and other dairy products
Tools and equipment for house and garden
Spare parts and accessories for motor vehicles
Equipment for sports, camping and open-air recreation
Domestic market services: Cleaning, repair and hire of clothing and footwear
Maintenance and repair of the dwelling
Maintenance and repair of motor vehicles
Audio, visual and computing media and services
Veterinary and other services for pets
Other recreational, sporting and cultural services

_comment: Classes whose inflation has a meaningful relationship with domestic
slack -- the unemployment gap, the underutilisation rate, the output gap
and capacity utilisation. In practice that is the labour-intensive
domestic services plus the housing channel: prices set by Australian
wages and Australian demand rather than by world prices, an excise
schedule or a regulator's determination. Everything else is
non-cyclical, including administered prices, tobacco and the tradables.
This is the classification most worth arguing with, and the chart says
so. Move a name between here and the residual and the two lines both
move -- which is the point of it being visible.
Deliberately the union of the `Domestic market services`, `Rent` and
`New dwelling purchase` buckets above, so the two classifications agree
with each other. Child care, dental and medical services and motor
vehicle registration are NOT here even though they are services: their
prices are set by a subsidy schedule or a regulator, which is the whole
reason they sit in `Administered prices` above. Free child care in June
2020 is the case that proves it -- a 95% fall in one quarter that no
reading of domestic slack predicts.
